title: The Problem with Patterns: How Good Data Leads to Bad Decisions
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau explains collider bias -- a statistical mechanism that generates false relationships in selected data -- through the lens of school behavior management. A headteacher's behavior lead found incident log clusters around specific corridors, times, and teachers, but the log is not a transcript of behavior -- it is a record of what was noticed, challenged, escalated, and written down. Teachers who trust the system and follow policy log more; those who don't trust escalation stop logging. When attention shifted to high-logging teachers, logging behavior changed and incident numbers fell -- not because behavior improved but because the metric was being managed. Collider bias (formalized by Berkson in 1946, developed through causal diagrams) arises when two causes share a common effect: conditioning on that effect creates false correlations between the causes. Examples: hospital samples make unrelated diseases appear inversely related (Berkson's paradox); university admissions make ability and wealth appear to trade off; dating apps make attractive people seem boring; Hollywood makes beautiful actors seem talentless; business studies of top salespeople who ignore the script mistake survivorship for genius. Schools are systematically vulnerable: every selected group they study (excluded students, persistently absent students, students in intervention) is the product of a selection process they then forget.
points: * A behaviour log is not a transcript of behavior -- it is a record of what was noticed, challenged, escalated, and written down; teachers who trust the system log more, those who don't trust escalation log less, creating a collider that makes high-compliance teachers appear to be a behavior problem. * Collider bias (Berkson, 1946): when two causes share a common effect, conditioning on that effect creates spurious correlations between the causes that would not exist in the general population. * The mechanism appears across domains: hospital populations (Berkson's paradox), university admissions (ability/wealth tradeoff), dating apps (attractive/interesting tradeoff), Hollywood (beautiful/talented tradeoff), business (successful rule-breakers look like geniuses). * Controlling for a confounder reduces bias; controlling for a collider creates it -- the distinction requires understanding the causal structure of the data, not just adding more variables to the analysis. * The professional lesson: the easy availability of data tempts schools to study spreadsheets instead of doing the hard work of visiting lessons, patrolling corridors, talking to teachers and students -- and asking which students are invisible, which policies are being followed versus worked around.
quotes: A behaviour log is not an accurate transcript of school life.
The school had mistaken a pattern for a cause.
Just as a map is not the territory, a behaviour log is not behaviour itself, but the paper trail it leaves behind.
Collider bias is a mechanism for manufacturing plausible falsehoods.
Although better analysis usually means controlling for more variables, this depends on understanding the difference between confounders and colliders.
The easy availability of data makes it tempting to study spreadsheets instead of doing the hard, dull work running a school.
Knowing about collider bias doesn't mean we should ignore evidence but that we should stop mistaking selected evidence for reality.
